title: Staying safely at home
headline: Make the home safer

noticed.text: {{name}} lives alone, so there may be no one nearby if something goes wrong.
You mentioned: {{homeConcerns}}.
The home may not have working smoke alarms.
{{name}} does not have a personal alarm to call for help.
There have been times when {{name}} has left home and become lost or confused.

whyItMatters: Small changes at home, such as working alarms, good lighting and a way to call for help, prevent many emergencies and make it more likely someone can keep living at home.

questions.question: Would {{name}} qualify for a funded personal alarm, and how do we arrange it?
Which changes in the home would make the biggest difference to safety?

information.title: Smoke alarms
information.body: Fire and Emergency New Zealand recommends long-life photoelectric smoke alarms in every bedroom, living area and hallway, and offers home fire safety advice.

actions.title: Fit working smoke alarms
actions.description: Install long-life photoelectric alarms in bedrooms, living areas and hallways, and test them.

actions.title: Arrange a personal alarm
actions.description: Ask the GP whether a funded personal alarm is available, or compare private monitored alarms.

actions.title: Agree a plan for when {{name}} goes missing
actions.description: Keep a recent photo and description ready, consider a location device, and tell close neighbours.

actions.title: Walk through the home for hazards
actions.description: Check lighting, loose mats, clutter on floors, and how easy it is to get in and out of the shower and bed.

title: Home care and support
headline: Get the right help at home

noticed.text: {{name}} currently has {{supportSummary}}.
{{name}} needs help with moving around, which makes personal care and daily tasks harder.
Taking medicines correctly has become difficult without help.

whyItMatters: The right mix of help, from a few hours of household support to daily personal care, is often what makes staying at home possible and safe.

questions.question: What funded home support could {{name}} be eligible for, and how long is the wait?
Could medicines be supplied in blister packs, and can the pharmacy review them?

information.title: Funded support starts with an assessment
information.body: Health New Zealand funds home support for eligible older people after a needs assessment by the local NASC service. A GP can make the referral.

actions.title: List the daily tasks that need help
actions.description: Note what is hard each day (showering, meals, shopping, medicines) so support can be matched to real needs.

actions.title: Ask the pharmacy about blister packs
actions.description: Pre-packed medicines by day and time reduce missed or doubled doses.

actions.title: Compare private home support while waiting
actions.description: If funded help will take time, a few privately paid hours can bridge the gap.

title: Falls and mobility
headline: Reduce the risk of another fall

noticed.text: {{name}} has had {{falls}} in the last 12 months.
{{name}} is worried about falling, which can lead to moving less and becoming weaker.
{{name}} uses a walking aid.

whyItMatters: One fall makes another more likely. Many falls can be prevented with a medication review, strength and balance exercise, and a safer home.

questions.question: Could any of {{name}}'s medicines be adding to dizziness or falls?
Should eyesight, blood pressure or bone health be checked after these falls?
Which strength and balance programme suits {{name}} now?

information.title: Strength and balance
information.body: Live Stronger for Longer lists community strength and balance classes around New Zealand, and GPs can refer people to an in-home programme.

actions.title: Book a GP falls review
actions.description: Ask for a medication review and checks of eyesight, blood pressure and feet.

actions.title: Start a strength and balance programme
actions.description: Find a local class or ask for a referral to an in-home programme.

actions.title: Ask for an occupational therapy home assessment
actions.description: An occupational therapist can recommend rails, seating and changes that make moving around safer.

title: Government funding
headline: Check the funding available

noticed.text: Paying for care is a significant worry for the family.
The family has some concerns about the cost of care.
The family is considering an application for the Residential Care Subsidy.

whyItMatters: Several government subsidies depend on assessments and applications that take time. Starting early avoids paying costs that could have been covered.

questions.question: Which subsidies or allowances could {{name}} be eligible for now?
Does {{name}}'s assessed level of care allow a subsidy application?

information.title: Residential Care Subsidy
information.body: Helps pay for long-term rest home or hospital care after a needs assessment. It is income and asset tested; as at 1 July 2026 the asset thresholds are $300,811 (Threshold A) and $164,731 (Threshold B), and they change each year.

information.title: Residential Care Loan
information.body: If assets are over the threshold mainly because of a home, a Residential Care Loan from Work and Income may help cover care costs.

actions.title: Check current entitlements
actions.description: Ask Work and Income which allowances apply, such as help with extra costs from a health condition.

actions.title: Start the Residential Care Subsidy application
actions.description: Gather income and asset details for the application; it can be backdated only in limited cases.

title: Needs assessment
headline: Get a needs assessment

noticed.text: {{name}} has not had a needs assessment yet.
A needs assessment has been requested but has not happened yet.

whyItMatters: Most funded support for older people in New Zealand, including home support, carer relief and residential care subsidies, starts with a needs assessment by the local NASC service.

questions.question: Can you refer {{name}} for a needs assessment, and how urgent should we say it is?
Can family be present at the assessment, and what should we bring?

information.title: How assessments work
information.body: A NASC assessor visits to understand daily needs, health and support, then coordinates the services the person is eligible for.

actions.title: Ask the GP for a NASC referral
actions.description: Request a needs assessment and explain the main concerns in this plan.

actions.title: Confirm the assessment date
actions.description: Call the NASC service to check the referral arrived and ask for a date.

actions.title: Prepare for the assessment
actions.description: Write down the hardest parts of each day, recent events and what the family can and cannot do.

title: Dementia and memory changes
headline: Respond to memory changes

noticed.text: {{name}} has a diagnosis of dementia.
The family has noticed memory or thinking changes, but there is no diagnosis yet.
{{name}} has sometimes become lost or left home unexpectedly.

whyItMatters: An early assessment opens the door to support, treatment of other causes, and planning while {{name}} can still take part in decisions.
whoCanHelp: Alzheimers New Zealand or Dementia New Zealand local services

questions.question: Could these changes have another cause, such as medication, infection or low mood?
Should {{name}} be referred to a memory service or specialist?

information.title: Local dementia support
information.body: Alzheimers New Zealand and its member organisations offer information, education and support for people living with dementia and their families.

actions.title: Book a GP memory assessment
actions.description: Describe specific examples of the changes and when they started.

actions.title: Contact a local dementia support service
actions.description: Ask about education sessions, day programmes and support for family carers.

actions.title: Set up memory supports at home
actions.description: A large clock and calendar, labelled cupboards and a regular daily routine reduce confusion.

title: Hospital discharge
headline: Plan a safe return home

noticed.text: {{name}} is in hospital{{hospitalReason}}{{dischargeText}}.
{{name}} came home from hospital recently{{hospitalReason}}.

whyItMatters: The first weeks after hospital carry the highest risk of another admission. A clear plan for support, medicines and follow-up makes a safe return much more likely.

questions.question: What support will {{name}} need at home, and who will arrange it before discharge?
Which medicines have changed, and why?
What follow-up appointments are booked, and who do we call if things go wrong?

actions.title: Ask for a discharge planning conversation
actions.description: Meet the ward team before discharge to agree support, equipment and follow-up.

actions.title: Confirm support is in place for the first two weeks
actions.description: Check who visits, when, and what happens if support does not arrive.

actions.title: Check medicines against the discharge letter
actions.description: Remove stopped medicines from the home and ask the pharmacist to review the new list.

title: Respite
headline: Arrange regular breaks for the carer

noticed.text: {{carer}} has not yet had a planned break from caring.
Some respite has been used, but more regular breaks may be needed.

whyItMatters: Regular breaks protect the carer's own health, and that is often what keeps care at home sustainable.

questions.question: Is {{carer}} eligible for the Carer Support Subsidy, and how can it be used?

information.title: Carer Support Subsidy
information.body: Reimburses part of the cost of a break for full-time unpaid carers. It is allocated through a NASC needs assessment and can pay for a relief carer, a day programme or short residential respite.

information.title: Planning breaks
information.body: The Ministry of Social Development's guide for carers explains respite options and how to plan them.

actions.title: Ask about the Carer Support Subsidy
actions.description: Raise it at the needs assessment or call the NASC service directly.

actions.title: Book a first short break
actions.description: Start with a few hours or a day programme so everyone gets used to it.

title: Support for the family carer
headline: Support {{carer}} as the main carer

noticed.text: {{carer}} ({{carerRelationship}}) is the main carer.
{{carer}} is under a lot of strain and may be close to exhaustion.

whyItMatters: Family carers often put their own health last. If the main carer becomes unwell, the whole care arrangement can fall apart quickly.

questions.question: Can {{carer}} have a health check that takes the caring role into account?

information.title: Carers NZ
information.body: Carers NZ provides information, advice and peer support for family carers.

actions.title: Book a health check for {{carer}}
actions.description: Mention the caring role, sleep and stress so the GP can help.

actions.title: Share caring tasks across the family
actions.description: Agree who covers appointments, shopping, paperwork and regular visits.

title: EPOA and legal planning
headline: Put legal decision-making in place

noticed.text: An Enduring Power of Attorney for property is {{epoaPropertyText}}.
An Enduring Power of Attorney for personal care and welfare is {{epoaWelfareText}}.
Both Enduring Powers of Attorney are in place.
There is no advance care plan recording {{name}}'s wishes.

whyItMatters: An EPOA can only be made while a person can still understand it. Without one, the family may need to apply to the Family Court to make decisions, which takes time and money.
whoCanHelp: Te Tari Kaumātua Office for Seniors

questions.question: What does {{name}} need to set up both EPOAs, and how long will it take?
Is {{name}} able to make and sign an EPOA now?

information.title: Two kinds of EPOA
information.body: One covers property and money, the other covers personal care and welfare. A welfare EPOA only comes into effect if the person is assessed as no longer able to make decisions.

information.title: Making an EPOA
information.body: Te Tari Kaumātua publishes the standard forms and explains how they must be witnessed.

information.title: Advance care planning
information.body: An advance care plan records what matters most to a person about future care, so family and clinicians can follow their wishes.

actions.title: Set up both EPOAs with a lawyer
actions.description: Book a lawyer and choose attorneys for property and for personal care and welfare.

actions.title: Find existing legal documents
actions.description: Check with the family lawyer or trustee company whether an EPOA or will already exists, and keep copies.

actions.title: Start an advance care plan
actions.description: Talk with {{name}} and the GP about what matters most, and write it down.

title: Financial considerations
headline: Understand the costs ahead

noticed.text: The family has a guide budget of about ${{weeklyBudget}} a week for care or accommodation.
{{name}} owns their home, which affects subsidies and how a move could be funded.

whyItMatters: Retirement villages and residential care have very different costs and contracts. Understanding them early avoids rushed decisions.

questions.question: How would each option affect {{name}}'s income and assets over five years?

actions.title: Write a simple money snapshot
actions.description: List income, savings, regular costs and the value of the home, so options can be compared.

actions.title: Get independent financial advice
actions.description: A free budgeting service or a financial adviser can explain the options.

title: Transport
headline: Keep getting out and about

noticed.text: Getting to appointments and shops has become difficult.
{{name}} still drives, although there are concerns about memory.

whyItMatters: Losing transport often leads to missed appointments and isolation. Subsidised options can keep someone independent.

questions.question: Is {{name}} still safe to drive, and should a driving assessment be done?

information.title: Total Mobility
information.body: Subsidised taxi and ride-share fares for people who cannot use public transport safely because of an impairment. Eligibility is assessed by an approved agency and subsidies vary by region.

actions.title: Check eligibility for Total Mobility
actions.description: Ask the GP or a local agency about an assessment.

actions.title: Ask the GP about driving safety
actions.description: Discuss whether a driving assessment is needed.

title: Social connection
headline: Stay connected with others

noticed.text: {{name}} is often alone and has little contact with others.
{{name}} sees people less often than before.

whyItMatters: Loneliness affects mood, memory and physical health. One regular activity each week makes a real difference.

information.title: Visiting services
information.body: Age Concern runs visiting and social programmes for older people in many parts of New Zealand.

actions.title: Find one regular weekly activity
actions.description: A club, class, church group or day programme that {{name}} would enjoy.

actions.title: Check hearing and eyesight
actions.description: Untreated hearing or vision loss often makes social contact harder.

title: Retirement villages
headline: Explore retirement village options

noticed.text: {{name}} is interested in moving to a retirement village{{timeframeText}}.

whyItMatters: Villages differ a lot in costs, contracts and the care they offer later. The contract, called an occupation right agreement, needs careful reading before anyone signs.
whoCanHelp: Te Ara Ahunga Ora Retirement Commission

questions.question: What happens if {{name}} later needs rest home or hospital care?
What are the weekly fees, and how can they change?
What will {{name}} get back when leaving the village, and when?

information.title: Legal advice is required
information.body: Anyone buying into a registered village must get independent legal advice before signing the occupation right agreement, and has a cooling-off period after signing.

actions.title: Shortlist and visit three villages
actions.description: Compare fees, contracts, care on site and how far each is from family.

actions.title: Get independent legal advice on the contract
actions.description: Ask a lawyer to explain the occupation right agreement and disclosure statement before signing.

title: Residential care
headline: Prepare for a move into care

noticed.text: {{name}} has been assessed as needing {{assessedLevel}}-level care.
The family is considering residential care{{timeframeText}}.

whyItMatters: Choosing a care home is easier with time to visit, compare and apply for funding, rather than deciding during a crisis.

questions.question: Do you have a vacancy at {{assessedLevel}} level, and what are the extra charges?
How do you support new residents and families in the first weeks?

information.title: Levels of care
information.body: Aged residential care in New Zealand is provided at rest home, hospital, dementia and psychogeriatric levels. The level is confirmed by a needs assessment.

actions.title: Confirm the level of care needed
actions.description: A needs assessment decides whether rest home, hospital or dementia level care is right.

actions.title: Visit care homes and check vacancies
actions.description: Visit at least two homes at different times of day, and ask about extra charges.

title: Equipment and home changes
headline: Get the right equipment

noticed.text: The home has stairs {{name}} needs to use.
Moving around the home safely needs some support.

whyItMatters: Rails, shower seats and the right mobility aids are low-cost changes that prevent falls and keep people independent for longer.

questions.question: Which equipment is funded, and which would we need to buy?

actions.title: Fit bathroom rails and a shower seat
actions.description: The bathroom is the most common place for falls at home.

actions.title: Add rails on both sides of stairs
actions.description: Make sure stairs are well lit, with rails that can be gripped firmly.

title: Emergency planning
headline: Be ready for an emergency

noticed.text: If {{carer}} became unwell suddenly, there is no backup plan for {{name}}'s care.
In an emergency, responders may not know {{name}}'s medicines or who to contact.

whyItMatters: A one-page emergency sheet and a backup carer plan save precious time when something unexpected happens.

information.title: Emergency kits
information.body: Get Ready explains how to prepare a household emergency plan, including medicines and mobility needs.

actions.title: Make a one-page emergency sheet
actions.description: List medicines, conditions, allergies and contacts, and keep it on the fridge.

actions.title: Agree a backup plan if the main carer is unwell
actions.description: Decide who steps in, and how respite could be arranged at short notice.

title: Future planning
headline: Plan ahead while there is time

noticed.text: The family has not yet decided on longer-term living arrangements.
{{name}}'s goals: {{goals}}.

whyItMatters: Talking about wishes before a crisis means future decisions reflect what {{name}} wants.

actions.title: Have a family conversation about the future
actions.description: Talk about where {{name}} would like to live and what matters most.

actions.title: Review this plan in six months
actions.description: Update the plan if anything changes sooner.
